UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                      BEFORE THE
                        FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                                                           )
Forza Pipeline LLC                                         )           Docket No. CP26-34-000
Bull Run Pipeline LLC                                      )           Docket No. CP26-35-000

   JOINT MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER AND JOINT ANSWER OF FORZA
PIPELINE LLC AND BULL RUN PIPELINE LLC IN RESPONSE TO COMMENTS OF
HALEY FAMILY PROPERTY OWNERS ON THE ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT

           Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission's (“FERC”

or “Commission”) Rules of Practice and Procedure, 18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212, 385.213, Forza Pipeline

LLC (“Forza”) and Bull Run Pipeline LLC (“Bull Run”) (collectively, “Joint Applicants”) hereby

move for leave to answer (1) the comments filed on September 28, 2026 by Spanish Dagger, Ltd.,

SHER Cow Country, L.P., and Loving Cow Country, L.P. (collectively, “Property Owners”);1 and

(2) the comments dated September 28, 2026, from the State of New Mexico Department of

Wildlife (“NMDW”) (“EA Comments” and “NMDW EA Comments” respectively).                     The

comments were filed on the Environmental Assessment (“EA”) issued by Commission staff on

August 28, 2026 for the Forza Pipeline Project (“Forza Project” or “Project”).

           The EA Comments filed by the Property Owners largely restate arguments the Property

Owners raised in their January 6, 2026 Motion to Intervene and Protest and their February 27,

2026 Scoping Comments—arguments Joint Applicants addressed in their January 27, 2026 Joint

Answer (“Joint Answer”) and March 30, 2026 Response to Scoping Comments (“Response to

Scoping Comments”). As explained below, the EA itself directly addresses each of the concerns

the Property Owners now revisit, and their comments do not identify any deficiency in the EA or




1
    “Haley Property” refers to land held by the Property Owners.
 provide a basis to delay action on the Application. Joint Applicants also address the NMDW EA

Comments below.

         Joint Applicants respectfully request that the Commission accept this Answer and issue the

authorizations requested in the Application as expeditiously as practicable to permit Forza to

complete Project development and construction.

    I.      ANSWER TO PROPERTY OWNERS’ COMMENTS

         A. The EA Properly Analyzed the Project's Purpose and Need and the No-Action
            Alternative.

         The Property Owners contend that the EA “does not independently evaluate project need” and,

as a result, improperly “assumes the answer” when rejecting the no-action alternative. EA

Comments at 6. That argument mischaracterizes applicable legal standard, the EA's purpose-and-

need discussion and the record.

         In an EA, FERC must define the purpose of a project and consider reasonable alternatives—

including a no-action alternative—to the proposed project “that are technically and economically

feasible, and meet the purpose and need of the proposal.”2 FERC has considerable discretion

when defining the “purpose” of a project as the “definition of purpose is subject to a ‘rule of

reason.’”3 While the Commission may neither “define the objectives of its action in terms so

unreasonably narrow that only one alternative from among the environmentally benign ones in the

agency's power would accomplish the goals of the agency's action,” nor “frame its goals in terms




2
  42 U.S.C. § 4332 (C)(iii) (emphasis added); see also FERC, Staff Guidance Manual On Implementation of the
National Environmental Policy Act (2025) at 7 (an EA should briefly discuss the “[p]urpose and need for the proposed
action, as informed by the goals of the applicant, and based on the Commission’s statutory authority under the NGA,
FPA, or other appropriate statute.”).
3
  Citizens Action Coal. of Ind., Inc. v. FERC, 125 F.4th 229, 237 (D.C. Cir. 2025) (quoting Nat. Res. Def. Council,
Inc. v. Morton, 458 F.2d 827, 834 (D.C. Cir. 1972)); see also Seven Cnty. Infrastructure Coal. v. Eagle Cnty. Colo.,
605 U.S. 168, 181 (“an agency exercises substantial discretion” when “identify[ing] . . . feasible alternatives.”).


                                                         2
 so unreasonably broad that an infinite number of alternatives would accomplish those goals,”4

FERC “should take into account the needs and the goals of the parties involved in the application”

when defining the purpose of a proposed project.5 Moreover, when defining the purpose where

“FERC is considering a private proposal,” as is the case here, “it ‘may accord substantial weight

to the preferences of the applicant . . . in the siting and design of the project.’”6

    Contrary to Property Owners’ claims,7 the D.C. Circuit recognizes that the purpose of pipeline

projects before FERC can be appropriately defined with the needs and goals of the applicant

without improperly foreclosing consideration of the no-action alternative (i.e., Certificate denial).8

Furthermore, when considering such no-action alternatives, it is well-established that FERC may

reject them because the purpose and need of the project would not be fulfilled.9


4
  Conservation Found. v. FERC, 111 F.4th 42, 57 (D.C. Cir. 2024) (citations omitted).
5
  Citizens Against Burlington, Inc. v. Busey, 938 F.2d 190, 196 (D.C. Cir. 1991).
6
  Citizens Action Coal. of Ind., Inc. v. FERC, 125 F.4th 229, 237 (D.C. Cir. 2025) (quoting City of Grapevine v. Dep’t
of Transp., 17 F.3d 1502, 1506 (D.C. Cir. 1994)); see also Indep. Pipeline Co., 91 FERC ¶ 61,102, at 61,345 (2000)
(“In identifying and defining a project's objective and goal for NEPA purposes, the Commission generally adopts the
project sponsor's proposal in the NGA Section 7 application that implicates the need to conduct the environmental
review.”).
7
  EA Comments at 6 (claiming that because “the EA [] rejected the no-action alternative finding that without the
Project, the purpose and need would not be met” somehow violates NEPA because “[t]hat conclusion assumes the
answer” and leads to “the no-action alternative fail[ing] automatically.”).
8
  N.J. Conservation Found. v. FERC, 111 F.4th 42, 57-58 (D.C. Cir. 2024) (concluding that FERC's narrow definition
of the project did not foreclose consideration of denial of the Certificate, i.e., the no-action alternative where the EIS
describes the project's purpose of delivering “an incremental 829,400 dekatherms per day (Dth/d) of year-round firm
transportation capacity from the Marcellus Shale production area in northeastern Pennsylvania to delivery points in
Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and Maryland.”) (citation omitted).
9
  Ctr. for Biological Diversity v. FERC, 67 F.4th 1176, 1182 (D.C. Cir. 2023) (“FERC rejected this true no-action
alternative because it would not fulfill the Project’s purpose, which is to commercialize natural gas from Alaska’s
North Slope . . . FERC’s concise rejection of this [no-action] alternative was reasonable because the Project’s purpose
was commercialization of North Slope gas.”); Fuel Safe Wash. v. FERC, 389 F.3d 1313, 1326-27 (10th Cir. 2004)
(“The FEIS also rejected the no action alternative because the need for the project would not be fulfilled . . . Given
our deferential standard of review, we conclude that the FEIS adequately considered alternatives and was not arbitrary
or capricious”); Gas Transmission Nw., L.L.C. v. FERC, 157 F.4th 674, 693, 710-11 (5th Cir. 2025) (FERC rejected
alternatives including the no-action alternative as it “failed to meet the project’s stated purpose and objectives” among
other reasons. The court rejected project opponents’ assertions that FERC did not adequately consider the no-action
alternative. Discussing Seven Cnty. Infrastructure Coal. v Eagle Cnty. Colo., 605 U.S. 168 (2025), the court upheld
FERC’s no-action consideration because “FERC explained…that the ‘no action’ alternative would result in the
[proposed] project not taking place” and that the “most likely outcome would then be that the environmental
consequences of that project would not have occurred” and because FERC then described both “the existing state of
each resource, i.e., the no-action alternative” and “how the project would impact that status quo.”).


                                                            3
      Here, the EA identified the Project's purpose—providing new firm interstate takeaway capacity

from the Delaware Basin production area to multiple delivery points at or near the Waha Hub—

and expressly considered and rejected the no-action alternative. EA § A.2; EA § C.1.

     As Joint Applicants have twice explained in this docket, the Property Owners' “Waha is

oversupplied” theory misstates the Project's need case. Joint Answer at 2–4; Response to Scoping

Comments at 2–3. The Project is designed to relieve upstream takeaway constraints downstream

of the Red Hills and Copperhead processing facilities in the Delaware Basin—not to remedy a

supply shortage at Waha. As documented in the Application and the independent Forza Market

Study prepared by Brown, Williams, Moorehead & Quinn, Inc., existing residue-gas transportation

capacity out of the Delaware Basin is projected to be exceeded by growing production, and Waha

remains the transportation hub through which that gas reaches Gulf Coast, LNG export, power

generation, and industrial demand centers. Application at 18; Application Ex. I-2, Forza Market

Study at 6–11. The Commission has recognized that “new natural gas infrastructure . . . is critical

for the immediate term to help address pressing nationwide reliability and resource adequacy

concerns.” Interstate Nat. Gas Ass'n of Am., 191 FERC ¶ 61,209, at P 10 (2025).

     The Property Owners' repetition of their prior Waha-focused theory—without engaging with

the upstream constraints Forza actually identified—does not undermine the EA's purpose-and-

need discussion. Nor does it disturb the demonstrated market need reflected in binding precedent

agreements covering 87 percent of Project capacity, which the Commission has long recognized

as “the best evidence” of demand for a project's service.10 Unsupported assertions and speculative




10
   Adelphia Gateway, LLC, 169 FERC ¶ 61,220, at P 35 (2019); see also Myersville Citizens for a Rural Cmty., Inc.
v. FERC, 783 F.3d 1301, 1310–11 (D.C. Cir. 2015); City of Oberlin, Ohio v. FERC, 937 F.3d 599, 605–06 (D.C. Cir.
2019).


                                                       4
 counter-narratives are not a substitute for record evidence and cannot displace binding precedent

agreements as the best evidence of need for the Project.

     The EA's rejection of the no-action alternative follows directly from the record. Under the no-

action alternative, the Project would not be constructed, and Forza “would be unable to meet the

Project's stated purpose and need.” EA § C.1. The EA further recognized that customers could

seek other, potentially higher-impact transportation options. Id. The Property Owners' assertion

that the EA “assumes the answer” is nothing more than disagreement with the EA's conclusion; it

does not identify any procedural or analytical defect.

     Thus, FERC has “take[n] into account the needs and the goals of the [Joint-Applicants]

involved in the application,”11 defining the purpose of the Project well within “rule of reason.”12

Then, the Commission adequately considered and reasonably rejected the no-action alternative

that fails to fulfil the purpose of the Project in compliance with NEPA.13

     B. The EA Properly Considers the Bull Run Extension.

     The Property Owners renew their claim that FERC has “segmented” review of the Forza

Project by not conducting joint NEPA review of the intrastate Bull Run Extension. EA Comments

at 6–8. Property Owners are wrong for both legal and factual reasons.




11
   Citizens Against Burlington, Inc. v. Busey, 938 F.2d 190, 196 (D.C. Cir. 1991).
12
   Citizens Action Coal. of Ind., Inc. v. FERC, 125 F.4th 229, 237 (D.C. Cir. 2025) (quoting Nat. Res. Def. Council,
Inc. v. Morton, 458 F.2d 827, 834 (D.C. Cir. 1972)).
13
   See, e.g., Ctr. for Biological Diversity v. FERC, 67 F.4th 1176, 1182 (D.C. Cir. 2023); Fuel Safe Wash. v. FERC,
389 F.3d 1313, 1326-27 (10th Cir. 2004); Gas Transmission Nw., L.L.C. v. FERC, 157 F.4th 674, 693, 710-11 (5th
Cir. 2025). See also 42 U.S.C. § 4332(C)(iii) (“a reasonable range of alternatives to the proposed agency action . . .
that are technically and economically feasible, and meet the purpose and need of the proposal.”) (emphasis added);
FERC, Staff Guidance Manual On Implementation of the National Environmental Policy Act (2025) at 11 (instructing
that “the purpose and need for the proposed action” should be “informed by the goals of the applicant, and based on
the Commission’s statutory authority under the NGA . . . or other appropriate statute” and noting that reasonable
alternatives “are technically and economically feasible, and meet the purpose and need of the proposal.”) (emphasis
added).


                                                          5
      First, the EA explains that it was prepared to “evaluate the environmental impacts of Forza

Pipeline LLC’s (Forza) and Bull Run Pipeline LLC’s (Bull Run) proposed Forza Pipeline Project

(Project).” EA at A.1. In addition to the Forza pipeline construction, the EA addressed the request

to enter into a capacity lease agreement pursuant to which Forza would lease 750,000 Dth/d of

natural gas transportation from Bull Run. EA at i, 1. FERC concluded that this authorization “does

not involve Commission-jurisdictional construction or modification of physical facilities and, by

itself, does not result in environmental effects.” EA at 1. In turn, “[t]he EA addresses only the

jurisdictional construction and operation proposed [for Forza] and does not further analyze the

lease request[.]” EA at 1-2. Nevertheless, the EA does consider construction of the Bull Run

Extension in its analysis of “environmental trends and planned activities.” EA at 11-13. In that

discussion, the EA identifies “reasonably foreseeable” activities that “may influence the

environmental baseline in which the Project would be constructed.” Those activities include the

Bull Run Extension. EA at 12.

     Second, the EA does not improperly “segment” construction of the Bull Run Extension from

the Forza Pipeline. Improper “segmentation” may occur when “connected actions” are not

considered in the same environmental document.14 However, “connected actions” must be actions

within the jurisdiction of the agency and pending at the same time.15 Here, the Bull Run Extension

is fully permitted, fully constructed, anticipated to be ready to go into service in October of 2026,

and is not within FERC’s jurisdiction. Joint Applicants have twice explained why Property

Owners’ argument on this point is wrong and incorporate their prior discussion by reference. Joint


14
   See e.g., Meyersville Citizens for a Rural Cmty., Inc. v. FERC, 783 F.3d 1301, 1326 (D.C. Cir. 2015) (“the
Commission is required to include “connected actions”…in an Environmental Assessment,” and “An agency
impermissibly ‘segments’ NEPA review when it divides connected…actions into separate projects…”).
15
   See Sierra Club v. FERC, 153 F.4th 1295, 1308 (D.C. Cir. 2025) (quoting Seven Cnty. Infrastructure Coal. v. Eagle
Cnty., Colorado, 605 U.S. 168, 188 (2025) (“Seven County”)) (“In sum, after Seven County, agencies are no longer
‘required to analyze the effects of projects over which they do not exercise regulatory authority.’”).


                                                         6
 Answer at 6–9; Response to Scoping Comments at 13–14. Nevertheless, Property Owners have

again failed to acknowledge that the Bull Run project is not within FERC’s jurisdiction, provide

no case law to support their position, and ignore controlling authority from the U.S. Supreme

Court.

     The EA explains that the Bull Run Extension is a non-jurisdictional facility and assesses

whether Bull Run “may be integral to the need for the proposed facilities” or merely “non-integral

components of the proposed facilities.” See EA at 9. In determining that the “Bull Run

Extension…do[es] not influence the location or configuration of the jurisdictional Project facilities

addressed in this EA,” the Commission reiterated that “the Bull Run Extension will be constructed

regardless of the Forza Project and that the Extension was developed to provide service to shippers

other than the Forza Project Shippers.” EA at 9.

     This is consistent with Supreme Court precedent. In Seven County Infrastructure Coalition v.

Eagle County, Colorado, 605 U.S. 168 (2025), the Supreme Court held that NEPA does not require

an agency to “analyze the effects of projects over which [it does] not exercise regulatory

authority.”16 The D.C. Circuit has since confirmed that “after Seven County, agencies are no longer

required to analyze the effects of projects over which they do not exercise regulatory authority.”17

     The Bull Run Extension is an intrastate natural gas pipeline subject to the jurisdiction of the

Railroad Commission of Texas (“RRC”). Bull Run has provided notice of construction to the

RRC,18 and construction of the Bull Run Extension will proceed regardless of whether the

Commission acts on the Forza Application.19 Additionally, the Bull Run Extension is planned to

18

                                                      7
 be placed in service approximately one year before the Forza Project. Application at 11. Bull

Run's own request for a limited-jurisdiction certificate to permit the transportation of interstate

natural gas over its intrastate facilities does not confer jurisdiction over the construction or

operation of the Bull Run Extension itself, and the Commission routinely categorically excludes

such capacity-lease authorizations from NEPA review.20 Thus, Seven County, together with Sierra

Club21 and the other post-Seven County D.C. Circuit decisions the Commission has relied on,

forecloses the Property Owners' contention that these Projects have been improperly segmented

for purposes of NEPA.22

     Nor is the Property Owners' new “pipeline to nowhere” framing a NEPA argument at all.

Whether the Forza Project's shippers can economically move gas out of the interconnection point

at Wildcat Junction absent the Bull Run Extension is a commercial question addressed by the

precedent agreements underlying the Project—agreements the Commission has repeatedly

recognized as the best evidence of need.23 And in any event, the Bull Run Extension has been

identified as a reasonably foreseeable future action and included in the Project's cumulative

impacts analysis. Resource Report 1, Appendix 1F; Response to Scoping Comments at 14. The

Property Owners' segmentation claim has no support in current law or in the record.

     C. NEPA Analysis is not a Vehicle for Assessing Economic Impacts to Property Owners
        and Compensation.

     The Property Owners’ comments reveal that their fundamental concern is the alleged economic

impact on the value of alleged caliche resources, wells, ranching operations, and land management

L.L.C., 163 FERC ¶ 61,123, P 18 (2018); Washington 10 Storage Corp., 175 FERC ¶ 61,051, at P 56 (2021).

 operations – in other words, the alleged fiscal impact of the project on their business operations.

However, NEPA analysis is not a tool to negotiate compensation. “NEPA requires agencies to

focus on the environmental effects of the project at issue.”24 While “socioeconomic impacts” may

be considered, “NEPA does not require an agency [to] examine the economic consequences of its

actions.”25     These parameters make sense given “[t]he purpose of NEPA is to protect the

environment, not the economic interests of those adversely affected by agency decisions.”26 The

D.C. Circuit routinely rejects claims brought under NEPA as failing to have a valid cause of action

where the interests at issue are economic rather than environmental.27

     Throughout the Property Owners’ EA comments and various requests for relief,28 it is apparent

that their true concerns lie in their economic interests rather than environmental impacts. For

instance, when talking about caliche, Property Owners discuss harms in terms of economic losses

related to the existing caliche pits and potential future losses.29                      Property Owners demand

compensation “for full damages” or else state that “the Commission must deny the certificate.”30

Similarly, when discussing purported impacts from invasive species, Property Owners state that

their $4,000 per year costs for controlling invasive species will increase due to the Project and that

 Property Owners should be compensated for “added costs to mitigate African rue.”31 And when

expressing concerns about potential impacts to ranching activities, Property Owners request that

the Commission require Forza to “fully compensate the Property Owners for…interference with

ranching activities.”32 Similarly, the Property Owners are concerned about having to truck water

or reduce the herd due to alleged impacts on water supply wells, a reduction in income due to

alleged impacts on salt water disposal wells, and seek compensation for alleged adverse effects on

ranching operations.33

     Taken together, Property Owners’ comments are focused on alleged financial impacts rather

than environmental impacts. But as explained above, NEPA does not require analysis of economic

impacts relative to uses of land.           Furthermore, FERC does not involve itself with setting

compensation to impacted landowners.34 Rather, compensation for an easement is negotiated

directly with the landowner. Where an easement is not negotiated then a state court obtains

jurisdiction upon commencement of a condemnation action and fair market value is set through

the state court process.35

     Notwithstanding the fact that NEPA doesn’t even require FERC to consider private

commercial interests, Property Owners’ allegations of interference with their ranching, caliche,

and water disposal operations are not supported by the evidence in the Forza project administrative

record. As detailed across multiple filings submitted by Joint Applicants, the Forza project is being

     D. The EA Adequately Analyzed the Project's Effects on Caliche Resources on the Haley
        Properties.

         EPA requires the Commission to consider reasonably foreseeable “significant

environmental impacts” of its proposed action but the Commission “exercises substantial

discretion” in doing so.37 This is because FERC “is better equipped to assess what facts are

relevant to [its] own decision than a court is.”38 Thus, so long as the Commission’s “choices…fall

within a broad zone of reasonableness” and are within “rule of reason,” then “Courts should afford

substantial deference and should not micromanage” the Commission’s EA.39 This deferential

standard is applicable to FERC’s approach on each concern raised by Property Owners and

discussed below.

         The Property Owners assert that the EA “does not analyze or even quantify the Project's

impact” to their caliche reserves and that Forza's route deviation to avoid pit operations actually

 “cuts through hundreds of thousands of cubic yards of unmined caliche.” EA Comments at 8–11.

Neither charge withstands the EA record.

           As an initial matter, as discussed above, NEPA is not the proper mechanism for Property

Owners to use to seek compensation for the project’s use of a right of way across Property Owners’

lands. Indeed, given the common presence of caliche in this area, any impacts to that resource are

unavoidable. If Property Owners believe impacts to the resource on their properties merit

compensation, they are free to raise that issue in the course of right of way negotiations or

condemnation proceedings.

           In any event, Property Owners’ assertions are misplaced and factually inaccurate. First,

Property Owners recognize that Forza’s route was revised to avoid the existing caliche mine but

now express concern that the pipeline will bisect or run in between the East End and West End

caliche pits. EA Comments at 9-10. These pits are thousands of feet apart.40 Property Owners do

not adequately explain how the project will foreclose access or expansion of accessible caliche

resources given the existing pipeline infrastructure already in the area that bisects the caliche pits

for which Forza would be co-located with. Thus, the foreseeability of impacts from Forza

specifically on hypothetical future caliche mining is questionable at best given the limitations from

existing infrastructure and Forza’s plan to minimize impacts via co-location. Moreover, the Forza

pipeline will run underneath current access roads to avoid impeding Property Owners’ access and

existing operations, minimizing purported impacts further.

       The Commission has adequately considered impacts to caliche resources when assessing both

the geological setting and mineral resources in the EA. EA at 13-14. The Commission recognizes

the Haley Property Owners’ generalized concerns related to stranding of caliche resources and



40

                                                  12
 explains that Haley Property Owners failed to provide specific locations for referenced caliche

deposits which prevented the Commission from determining “the exact area extent of overlapping

Project workspaces and reported caliche deposits.” EA at 14. Despite the lack of information

provided by the Haley Property Owners, the Commission noted that Forza submitted a “proposed

route in this area to specifically avoid caliche pit operations on the Haley property, and also

proposes to cross existing caliche operations access roads via subsurface bore to ensure access is

maintained during construction.” EA at 14. Thus, the Commission has adequately considered the

information provided by both Haley Property Owners and Forza related to caliche resources in

rendering the EA and should not be “excessively second-guessed.”41

       E. The EA Adequately Analyzed the Project's Effects on Water Wells and Saltwater
          Disposal Operations.

       The Property Owners next contend that the EA “does not analyze impacts to the Property

Owners' water wells” and “ignore[s]” their alleged saltwater disposal wells. EA Comments at 11–

12. That is incorrect.

       The EA sufficiently considers effects on saltwater disposal operations. See EA at 14. Setting

aside, as discussed above, Property Owners’ concerns on commercial viability of saltwater

disposal operations is not an environmental interest addressed by NEPA, the Commission does

acknowledge the Haley Property Owners’ concerns regarding two saltwater disposal wells

described as being located on either side of the proposed Project. However, the Commission

explains that the Haley Property Owners failed “to provide locations for the referenced disposal

      I. Forza's Right-of-Way Outreach Is Lawful and Does Not Presume Commission
        Determination.

     Finally, the Property Owners suggest that Forza's September 2, 2026, outreach letter regarding

right-of-way acquisition (EA Comments Exhibit 6) improperly “implies a condemnation authority

Forza does not yet have” and “pressures landowners to surrender their property rights before the

Commission has decided whether Forza may take them at all.” EA Comments at 18–19. That

characterization is inaccurate and misconstrues the nature of pre-certificate landowner

engagement.

     Pre-certificate outreach to affected landowners is a routine and expected part of the certificate

process. The Commission's Certificate Policy Statement expressly directs applicants to minimize

adverse landowner impacts and to negotiate right-of-way with affected landowners where

practicable. Certification of New Interstate Natural Gas Pipeline Facilities, 88 FERC ¶ 61,227,

at 61,748–50 (1999) (“Certificate Policy Statement”). Forza's outreach to the Property Owners is

consistent with that guidance and with Forza's extensive good-faith negotiation with all affected

landowners along the route, including the ongoing engagement with the Property Owners

themselves. Joint Answer at 11–13.

     Forza has not asserted, and has not exercised, any condemnation authority.55                             Forza

understands that eminent-domain authority attaches only after the Commission issues a certificate

of public convenience and necessity. Forza's September 2, 2026 letter is what it purports to be—

an acquisition offer initiating good-faith negotiation of easement terms. Nothing in the letter

forecloses the Property Owners' right to participate in this proceeding, and nothing in the letter

presumes a Commission determination.
